sources.title: Tagged JOIN/GROUP BY high-concurrency analytics coding question
Writer and reviewer SQLite grain/fan-out validation
Join/aggregate SQL candidate independent source-first review

claims.text: Schema, concrete metric, SQL dialect, SLA and concurrency target are not preserved by the source; the order example is explicitly illustrative.
Pre-aggregating one-to-many items to order grain prevents item multiplicity from inflating order-level count and revenue in the demonstrated contract.
The candidate does not claim generic index/QPS wins and instead requires target-database EXPLAIN and concurrent load validation for physical optimization choices.

boundary_tests.expected: order count remains order-grain while item rows are larger
boundary_tests.actual: writer gold 2 orders vs 3 item rows; reviewer segment a 3 orders vs 4 item rows

boundary_tests.expected: item values aggregate once per order then once per segment
boundary_tests.actual: writer 3500/900 and reviewer 550 match independent computations

boundary_tests.expected: paid order with no items excluded

findings: The source is intentionally broad and preserves no concrete schema, metric definition, database dialect, isolation level, freshness SLA or concurrency target; the candidate correctly labels its order/segment model as an illustrative answer-side contract.
The answer centers metric grain before syntax: one-to-many item fan-out is resolved by pre-aggregating to one row per order before the segment GROUP BY.

The writer fixture demonstrates 2 gold orders expanding to 3 item rows while still producing order_count=2 and revenue=3500; an independently authored fixture demonstrates 3 orders vs 4 item rows and independently computes revenue=550.
Status and half-open time filtering are tested, and the inner-join exclusion of paid orders without items is explicitly documented rather than silently treated as universal business behavior.

The high-concurrency section does not claim an unverified index or QPS result: it requires target-database execution-plan and load-test validation, and presents pre-aggregation/materialization/cache/read paths as options with freshness/consistency costs.
The candidate warns that COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) can repair order count without necessarily repairing duplicated order-level sums, which is the key semantic trap in this class of query.
No production experience or target-database performance result is fabricated.
